lesson.title: Er: The Little Word That Does Everything
lesson.subtitle: er is, er zijn, ik heb er twee — existence, place and 'of it'

hook.title: One Word, Four Jobs
hook.content: Er is the unstressed 'there'. It introduces existence (er is een boek), location (ik ben er), and quantity (ik heb er twee). It can also fuse with a preposition: erop, ermee, ervan.

pattern.title: Existential, locative, partitive
pattern.content: Er is/er zijn introduces something: er is een boek, er zijn twee boeken. Ik ben er means 'I am there'. Ik heb er twee means 'I have two of them'. The same little word covers all three.
pattern.linguist_note: Er descends from the same 'there' word as English there, but Dutch keeps an unstressed form for grammar while daar carries the stress.
pattern.trap_note: Use er zijn with a plural: er zijn twee boeken, not er is twee boeken.

exercises.prompt: Match each English meaning with its Dutch twin (Er: The Little Word That Does Everything):
exercises.target_answer: er, zijn, hebben, hier, daar, twee
exercises.meaning: there; of it/them, to be, to have, here, there, two
exercises.explanation: These are the anchors of "Er: The Little Word That Does Everything": read each Dutch form through the pattern, not as a new word.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence says: “There is a book.”?
exercises.explanation: “Er is een boek.” is the Dutch form; the other readings bend the pattern of “Er: The Little Word That Does Everything”.

cues: It means: There are two books.
exercises.explanation: “Er zijn twee boeken.” puts the thought together the Dutch way — Existential, locative, partitive.

diagnosis.slip: an English-shaped word order slipped in
diagnosis.cue: Use er zijn with a plural: er zijn twee boeken, not er is twee boeken.

exercises.prompt: Which English sentence is built the Dutch way?
exercises.explanation: “Ik heb er twee.” is word-for-word “I have there two.”. The odd English is the lesson — never a model to produce. Pattern: Existential, locative, partitive.

exercises.prompt: Listen and write the whole sentence.
exercises.explanation: “Ik ben er.” reuses only material taught in “Er: The Little Word That Does Everything” — Existential, locative, partitive.
exercises.affirmation: You heard “Ik ben er.” — a sentence built from the lesson's own Dutch, practising Existential, locative, partitive.

twist.prompt: One more, no safety net — say: “There is no water here.”
twist.explanation: Er introduces existence; geen negates the indefinite noun water.

summary.outcome: Use er for existence, location and 'of them'.
summary.takeaway: Er is the grammatical 'there' — a small word with several structural jobs.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Up next on De Brug: Er Gym.

er.etymology_derivation: The unstressed 'there' pronoun, with existential, locative and partitive jobs.

zijn.etymology_derivation: The being verb is irregular in every Germanic language; English is and Dutch is are the same old root.

hebben.etymology_derivation: English have and Dutch hebben descend from the same verb; the b is preserved.

hier.etymology_derivation: The same place word as English here.

daar.etymology_derivation: The same place word as English there; the d is the old th.

twee.etymology_derivation: English two and Dutch twee are the same word.
